question.text:
\[ \begin{cases} x'(t) = 2x(t)+y(t) \\[5pt] y'(t) = 2y(t) \end{cases} \] Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

Hint: $e^{At} = \begin{bmatrix} e^{2t} & te^{2t} \\ 0 & e^{2t} \end{bmatrix},$ where $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 &1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get \[ \mathbf{x}'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} 2 &1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}(t), \] where $\mathbf{x}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 &1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t) \, \mathbf{c}, \] where $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system is given by \[ \Phi_0(t) = e^{At} = \begin{bmatrix} e^{2t} & te^{2t} \\ 0 & e^{2t} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, the general solution is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x}(t) &=\Phi_0(t) \, \mathbf{c} \\[5pt] &= e^{At} \, \mathbf{c} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} e^{2t} & te^{2t} \\ 0 & e^{2t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= c_1\begin{bmatrix} e^{2t} \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + c_2\begin{bmatrix} te^{2t} \\ e^{2t} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= c_1\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} e^{2t} + c_2\begin{bmatrix} t \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} e^{2t}, \end{align*}

where $c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.$

question.text:
\[ \begin{cases} x'(t) = -4y(t) \\[5pt] y'(t) = 4x(t) \end{cases} \] Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

Hint: $e^{At} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(4t) & -\sin(4t) \\ \sin(4t) & \cos(4t) \end{bmatrix},$ where $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -4 \\ 4 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get \[ \mathbf{x}'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -4 \\ 4 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}(t), \] where $\mathbf{x}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -4 \\ 4 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t) \, \mathbf{c}, \] where $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system is given by \[ \Phi_0(t) = e^{At} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(4t) & -\sin(4t) \\ \sin(4t) & \cos(4t) \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, the general solution is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x}(t) &=\Phi_0(t) \, \mathbf{c} \\[5pt] &= e^{At} \, \mathbf{c} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \cos(4t) & -\sin(4t) \\ \sin(4t) & \cos(4t) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= c_1\begin{bmatrix} \cos(4t) \\ \sin(4t) \end{bmatrix} + c_2\begin{bmatrix} -\sin(4t) \\ \cos(4t) \end{bmatrix}, \end{align*}

where $c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.$

question.text:
\[ \begin{cases} x'(t) = -2y(t) \\[5pt] y'(t) = -2x(t) \end{cases} \] Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

Hint: $e^{At} = \begin{bmatrix} \cosh(2t) & -\sinh(2t) \\ -\sinh(2t) & \cosh(2t) \end{bmatrix},$ where $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get \[ \mathbf{x}'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}(t), \] where $\mathbf{x}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t) \, \mathbf{c}, \] where $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system is given by \[ \Phi_0(t) = e^{At} = \begin{bmatrix} \cosh(2t) & -\sinh(2t) \\ -\sinh(2t) & \cosh(2t) \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, the general solution is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x}(t) &=\Phi_0(t) \, \mathbf{c} \\[5pt] &= e^{At} \, \mathbf{c} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \cosh(2t) & -\sinh(2t) \\ -\sinh(2t) & \cosh(2t) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= c_1\begin{bmatrix} \cosh(2t) \\ -\sinh(2t) \end{bmatrix} + c_2\begin{bmatrix} -\sinh(2t) \\ \cosh(2t) \end{bmatrix}, \end{align*}

where $c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.$

question.text:
\[ \begin{cases} x'(t) = 6x(t)+y(t) \\[5pt] y'(t) = 6y(t), \end{cases} \qquad \begin{bmatrix} x(0) \\ y(0) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -4 \end{bmatrix} \] Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

Hint: $e^{At} = \begin{bmatrix} e^{6t} & te^{6t} \\ 0 & e^{6t} \end{bmatrix},$ where $A = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 1 \\ 0 & 6 \end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get \[ \mathbf{x}'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 1 \\ 0 & 6 \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}(t), \] where $\mathbf{x}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 1 \\ 0 & 6 \end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi_0(t) \, \mathbf{x}(0), \] where $\Phi_0(t) = e^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{x}(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system is given by

\[ \Phi_0(t) = e^{At} = \begin{bmatrix} e^{6t} & te^{6t} \\ 0 & e^{6t} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, the solution is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{x}(t) &= e^{At} \, \mathbf{x}(0) \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} e^{6t} & te^{6t} \\ 0 & e^{6t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -4 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -4te^{6t} \\ -4e^{6t}\end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t) \, \mathbf{c}, \] where $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi_0(t) \mathbf{c} =e^{At} \, \mathbf{c}, \] where $\Phi_0(t) = e^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t=t_0,$ we have \[ \mathbf{x}(t_0) = e^{At_0} \, \mathbf{c} \] and since $e^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have \[ \mathbf{c} = e^{-At_0} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0). \]

Plugging the above back into our expression for $\mathbf{x}(t),$ we get \begin{align*} \mathbf{x}(t) &= e^{At} \, e^{-At_0} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0) \\[5pt] &= e^{A(t-t_0)} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0). \end{align*}

Therefore, the solution is \begin{align*} \mathbf{x}(t) &= e^{A(t-1)} \, \mathbf{x}(1) \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \cos(4(t-1)) & \sin(4(t-1)) \\ -\sin(4(t-1)) & \cos(4(t-1)) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \hspace{2pt}\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{3\sin(4(t-1))} \hspace{2pt}\\ \hspace{2pt}\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{3\cos(4(t-1))} \hspace{2pt} \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}
